text:
The three days of travel in Genesis 22 may be read as a suspended sentence, in which nothing outward happens and everything of consequence is decided. The narrator dwells upon the servants, the wood, the knife, and the fire; and in naming them he names the instruments of the act before the act itself. Obedience and horror are kept together, and neither is suffered to prevail. Faith in this account is an arrangement of persons and obligations, and owes little to feeling.

Compared with the earlier promise, the scene differs from it less than it first appears. Isaac is the child of the covenant, through whom the nations are to be blessed; and that promise is now converted into a test. The weight of the scene rests on one word, hineni, "here I am," which Abraham speaks three times: to God, to Isaac, and to the angel. Each time it means something different, and each time it costs him more; in this story the language of presence is also the language of loss.
